entries.title: Apple Maps Adds ‘Lake America’ After Trump Personally Reached Out
entries.summary: The change happened the same day that Apple’s new CEO, John Ternus, began his tenure.
entries.content:
Apple Maps renamed Lake Ontario “Lake America” this week, just days after President Donald Trump reportedly contacted the technology company to urge the change.

Apple confirmed to Reuters that the name was changed on Tuesday following an update to the Geographic Names Information System, the federal database for nomenclature.

Trump signed an executive order Aug. 27 directing Interior Secretary Doug Burgum to rename Lake Ontario, one of the five Great Lakes, amid an escalating trade war with Canada. At the time Trump insisted he was sending “no message” to the northern neighbor with the order despite suggesting earlier that it was connected to failed negotiations on a trade deal.

The executive order says that because more of the lake’s volume lies within territory claimed by the U.S., Trump has the right to unilaterally change its name.

Name-change requests traditionally take months or even years to accomplish, though such conventions were upended after Trump’s second inauguration when he unilaterally renamed the Gulf of Mexico the “Gulf of America.” The rollout was chaotic as the White House pressured news media and the mapping divisions of Apple and Google to reflect the change.

The “Lake America” change appeared to have been smoother, even as some Republican leaders in the Midwest and Northeast pushed back against the order and Democrats vowed to not comply.

Burgum told Fox’s “Mornings with Maria” that Trump “reached out to Apple directly” about the name change, which happened the same day that Apple’s new CEO, John Ternus, began his tenure.

Apple did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Google said in a statement Sunday that it formally changed the name to “Lake America” as part of its policy to mirror official government sources. U.S-based users will see “Lake America,” Canada-based users will see Lake Ontario and users elsewhere in the world will see both names, the company added.

Apple is poised to follow a similar structure, according to Reuters.

entries.title: Pentagon Delays PFAS Cleanup at Over 200 Military Sites for the Third Time
entries.summary: This time, the Defense Department is telling lawmakers ahead of time that it plans to push back the forever chemical cleanup timelines.
entries.content:
The Pentagon is again delaying its timelines to clean up “forever chemicals” at hundreds of contaminated military sites across the United States, the third time in a year the department has extended estimates for completing a key phase of the cleanups.

The latest update will change the schedule at 243 installations, a senior Defense Department official told NOTUS on Wednesday. The official acknowledged that the dates at those installations are being pushed back, while arguing the changes should not be interpreted as a slowdown in the Pentagon’s effort to address contamination from the chemicals known as PFAS.

Instead, the official said the new dates reflect expanding investigations, evolving regulatory standards and additional work needed as the department learns more about contamination at individual sites.

“Every time we peel those things back, we find more work, and we continue to want to make sure that we get this right,” the official said.

The changes mark the latest setback in the Pentagon’s yearslong effort to address widespread PFAS contamination caused by decades of military use of firefighting foam at airfields and training facilities.

They also come after lawmakers and communities complained that the Pentagon had previously published revised dates online without a public announcement. Between May and June, the Pentagon quietly pushed back cleanup schedules at nearly 200 sites, as NOTUS first reported. Those delays included 15 military sites where PFAS contamination had already spread into the drinking water of nearby communities.

Two dozen senators subsequently demanded that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth reverse the delays and provide more information about how the decisions were made.

This time, the department is taking a different approach. Pentagon officials notified lawmakers and reporters ahead of the update and said installations will be expected to communicate the changes locally through public meetings, restoration advisory boards, social media and fact sheets.

“I can always communicate more effectively,” the senior official said, acknowledging the concerns about the department’s previous handling of the schedule changes.

The department also plans to change how cleanup information is conveyed on its website in an effort to be “more plain, more spoken, more addressing the issues, so communities can see what's happening,” the official said. The department is planning to roll out a site redesign later this year.

Defense officials insist the later dates do not mean the cleanup work is stopping. The Pentagon says it’s using interim measures — such as contaminated soil removal, groundwater treatment, filtration systems for homes and work with municipal water supplies — while longer investigations continue.

“I want to reiterate: It's not a pause in our efforts. In fact, the ongoing efforts are increasing,” the official said. “But these adjustments that you're going to see are based upon both the interim actions that we're taking on the cleanup part of this. Right, so we're taking more interim actions.”

The official said that the schedules are driven mainly by the science and the amount of investigative work required. Asked whether additional money from Congress could shorten the cleanup timelines, the official did not identify a specific funding level or say how much faster the work could proceed.

The military is one of the country’s most significant sources of PFAS pollution. PFAS, which stands for per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, can remain in the environment and the human body for decades. In large enough concentrations, the chemicals can cause health problems ranging from developmental issues to certain cancers.
entries.author: Joe Gould, Anna Kramer

entries.title: Trump Suggests Renaming the Strait of Hormuz
entries.summary: The president said he wants to call the waterway, which is critical to global trade, the “Trump Strait.”
entries.content:
President Donald Trump on Wednesday proposed naming the Strait of Hormuz after himself, a move that comes as he attempts to leave his mark on the global stage by renaming international bodies of water.

“Now that we have it under U.S.A. control, should we change the name Hormuz Strait to TRUMP STRAIT???” Trump wrote on Truth Social. “Like America itself, it would be “hotter” than ever before!”

The strait, through which one-fifth of the world’s oil passed before the war, remains a critical waterway for the global oil supply.

Unlike some of Trump’s previous efforts to rename bodies of water that border the U.S., the Strait of Hormuz is thousands of miles away from U.S. territory.

Trump’s suggestion to rename the strait comes days after he signed an executive order to change the name of Lake Ontario to “Lake America.” The controversial decision has drawn criticism, including from northern state Republicans whose jurisdictions border Canada, as Trump’s trade war with the country escalates.

Despite the pushback, some tech giants are following the president’s lead. Apple Maps, for example, acquiesced to the name change this week after the president personally reached out to the company. Google Maps changed the lake’s name shortly after Trump’s order last week.

He also renamed the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America earlier in his term — and though the change is reflected on Apple Maps, it is not widely recognized by Mexico or other countries.

Trump has repeatedly said that the U.S. has control of the Strait of Hormuz since the onset of the war in February — despite many instances of Iranian forces taking military action in the waterway.

The U.S. resumed major strikes against Iran earlier this week and targeted assets in the strait. Trump threatened Iran with the “biggest attack of them all,” but the country launched retaliatory strikes on U.S. allies in the region anyway, including on Jordan, Bahrain and Kuwait.

entries.title: $1 Coins Featuring Trump’s Face Are Now in Circulation
entries.summary: The front of the coins feature the president's image, and the presidential seal with a 250 inscription is on the back.
entries.content:
The U.S. Mint began selling $1 coins with President Donald Trump’s image on Wednesday, the latest instance of the president being added to federal government materials.

The coins, which were announced in July, are being rolled out to commemorate the nation’s 250th anniversary.

They are being priced well above their face value: Buyers can get 25 $1 coins for $61 or a 100-count bag for $154.50. There is a limit of two orders per household, and the website to buy the coins appears to be putting potential buyers in a virtual waiting room due to the high demand. As of publication, the wait time was listed as more than an hour.

Trump’s image has already been added to limited-edition U.S. passports and the national parks’ annual pass.

Living presidents typically do not appear on currency, but the Trump administration relied on a 2020 law that he signed during his first term to allow his portrait on the coin. The Circulating Collectible Coin Redesign Act allows the U.S. Mint, only in 2026, to issue “$1 dollar coins with designs emblematic of the U.S. semiquincentennial.”

But Trump is not the first sitting president to appear on a coin. In 1926, President Calvin Coolidge appeared on a half-dollar coin alongside George Washington to mark 150 years of the country’s independence — though the coin was intended to be a commemorative souvenir sold to the public, rather than to be used as currency like Trump’s coin.

“The coins — minted at the Philadelphia Mint — have circulating finishes but have never been placed into circulation. However, they may be still used as legal tender,” the U.S. Mint announced in its rollout of the $1 Trump coinage.

The U.S. Mint snuck 250,000 special-issue coins with a July 4th privy mark, or small symbol added to the currency, into some of the rolls and bags.

The Trump coin is gold-colored, but it is actually a mix of 88.5% copper with smaller quantities of zinc, manganese and nickel.

entries.title: Air Force Probing Iran War Widow’s ‘Missing’ Benefits
entries.summary: Libby Klinner said she was deemed ineligible for certain benefits because Congress had not officially declared war against Iran.
entries.content:
The Air Force is reviewing the case of a Gold Star widow from Alabama who wrote on social media that she was deemed ineligible for additional benefits following her husband’s death because Congress had not officially declared the military operations in Iran a war.

A spokesperson for the Air Force said in a statement that military officials spoke Monday with Libby Klinner, the wife of Maj. John Alexander Klinner, who was one of six service members killed when an aircraft crashed in Iraq during a refueling mission on March 12. The spokesperson added the Air Force wanted to ensure Klinner received “all eligible benefits she and her family are entitled to.”

“We remain committed to providing clear information and continued support to Mrs. Klinner, as well as all the families of the Airmen who died in the KC-135 crash,” the spokesperson’s statement said.

Libby Klinner said on her Instagram account over the weekend that her casualty assistance officer had informed her she would not receive additional benefits following her husband’s death “because we have not declared war.” Klinner said the extra benefits “missing” from her husband’s final paycheck were combat-pay related.

“So not only was my husband killed in a war he never wanted to participate in,” she wrote, “but now the benefits we’re left with are being dictated by semantics and public perception.”

Two days later, Klinner said the director of mortuary affairs informed her the Air Force was “initiating an audit on our benefits to ensure that we receive all that we are entitled to.”

The Air Force spokesperson said in a statement that they are “committed to addressing her concerns with care and respect,” but did not elaborate on why Klinner was initially told she was not entitled to the extra benefits. The Air Force did not answer questions on whether other Gold Star families have also experienced similar issues.

Military operations in Iran have spanned six months with no clear end in sight. At least 14 service members, including Klinner, have died, and more than 400 troops have been wounded in action as part of Operation Epic Fury.

The Pentagon does not count the deaths of four additional service members, all of whom were killed during an Iranian ballistic missile attack in Jordan in late July, as part of the operation’s fatality toll.

entries.title: State Lawmakers Demand Burgum Halt Plans to Give Part of Yosemite to a Developer
entries.summary: A bipartisan coalition of California lawmakers wrote to Burgum after NOTUS first reported on the administration's efforts to parcel off a piece of Yosemite.
entries.content:
A bipartisan coalition of California lawmakers demanded that the Trump administration “halt and reject” a proposed sale of part of Yosemite National Park to a private developer in a letter to Interior Secretary Doug Burgum on Wednesday.

The letter followed reporting by NOTUS that revealed National Park Service staff in California and Washington, D.C., have been trying to arrange a land exchange between a Nevada-based company and the federal government.

In the letter, prominent Republicans and Democrats in California’s state legislature told Burgum that “Yosemite is not a subdivision, and it is not for sale.” The lawmakers cited the Yosemite Grant Act, signed by President Abraham Lincoln in 1864, as the first time the federal government set aside scenic land for preservation and public use.

“The existence of a land-exchange mechanism does not make this an appropriate use of it. Protecting Yosemite requires no creative interpretation of federal law, just the judgment to say No,” the lawmakers said in the letter.

Signatories to the letter included both the California Assembly Speaker Robert Rivas and Republican Senate Minority Leader Brian W. Jones and totaled more than half of the California state legislature.

Since spring 2025, the Interior Department has been working with the real estate developer and investment firm Kingsbarn Realty Capital on a deal that would allow it to build a short road on Yosemite land, which would give the property rare private access to the park.

Kingsbarn, through a web of limited liability companies, owns an 83-acre parcel of land on the western edge of Yosemite’s boundaries. Currently the property’s only access to the National Park’s main attractions is via a long and circuitous road through Forest Service lands.

In an interview with The Washington Post, Jeff Pori, Kingsbarn CEO, said his company plans to build short-term rentals on the property. Pori confirmed NOTUS’ reporting that he is pursuing a land-exchange agreement with the Park Service and that the deal is currently waiting for a land appraisal.

Former park officials, the park’s staff union and national park advocates have led a chorus of opposition to this proposed plan.

The Interior Department has maintained that no final decisions have been made. Any deal “would be subject to all applicable federal laws, regulations, and Departmental policies, including required environmental review and public notification processes,” a spokesperson for the National Park Service said.
entries.author: Avani Kalra

entries.title: Plane Carrying DHS Secretary Makes Emergency Landing at DCA
entries.summary: A Coast Guard aircraft carrying Markwayne Mullin experienced engine failure Wednesday afternoon.
entries.content:
A Coast Guard airplane carrying Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin made an emergency landing at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport Wednesday afternoon after an engine failure.

The pilot told DCA’s control tower the plane lost its right engine and had 14 people on board, according to a recording of air traffic control audio. The plane, a Gulfstream jet, landed safely around 1:35 p.m. and did not cause disruption to any other flights, Metropolitan Washington Airports Authority spokesperson Crystal Nosal said in an email.

Mullin said in a post on social media that he was one of the people aboard. The plane is frequently used to transport the secretary and high-ranking members of the Coast Guard.

“The United States Coast Guard pilots made the single engine landing feel routine. No panic, just straight professionalism,” he wrote. “After we landed, the pilots told me that was a first for them! We could not have been in better hands.”

Last year, DHS said the plane, which is more than 20 years old, is too worn-out to remain in use and should be replaced as a matter of safety.

The Coast Guard declined to comment. The Department of Homeland Security directed questions to Mullin's social media post.

entries.title: Trump’s Great American Road Trip
entries.content:
Good afternoon. This is the Final NOTUS newsletter for Sept. 2, 2026. You can get it in your inbox every day by signing up here — it’s free!

THE LATEST

President Donald Trump says he’s going to do a blitz of campaign travel — in the last 30 days before an election that doesn’t necessarily favor his party. Trump didn’t specify how many states he’ll hit, just that he’ll “be making a lot of stops,” including one in Alaska with Sen. Dan Sullivan.

  • “Some people don’t like the way he dresses, or some people don’t like the way he interviews or talks,” Trump said of Ken Paxton before heaping praise on the Texas attorney general.
Jamieson Greer met with the Republican Study Committee at their weekly lunch today, joined by Mike Johnson. The U.S. trade representative recently said Canada could get hit with additional tariffs as trade negotiations between the countries have collapsed.

  • Rep. Zach Nunn (R-Iowa) said he and others voiced concerns about the administration’s decision to drop ground beef tariffs during the meeting and that he will deliver that message to the White House today, Semafor reports.
  • Nunn and several GOP lawmakers facing competitive races will dine with Trump in the Rose Garden tonight, Politico reports.




THE HILL

Outgoing Sen. Thom Tillis (R-North Carolina) urged Trump to replace Pete Hegseth, citing an article about military leaders leaving the administration in waves during the defense secretary’s tenure.

  • “I have never witnessed more inept management of the brave men and women who serve our country,” Tillis wrote in a post on X, asking the president “to find a new leader at the Pentagon who will retain and empower our military talent rather than diminish it.”
A bipartisan coalition of California lawmakers demanded that the Trump administration “halt and reject” a proposed sale of part of Yosemite National Park to a private developer in a new letter to Interior Secretary Doug Burgum.

The U.S.-Venezuela oil deal has raised red flags among House Republicans who fear that talks with acting President Delcy Rodríguez could ruin the chances of democratic elections in the country.

Democrats want to flip Republican Rep. Andy Barr’s Kentucky district — banking on an angry electorate to do so.





THE ADMINISTRATION

Trump suggested renaming the Strait of Hormuz after himself. Later this afternoon, he said he wasn’t serious about the proposition and was “just throwing it out there.”

  • Apple Maps relabeled Lake Ontario as “Lake America” this week, just days after Trump reportedly contacted the technology company to urge the change.
The Pentagon is again delaying its timelines to clean up “forever chemicals” at hundreds of contaminated military sites — the third time in a year the department has extended estimates for completing a key phase of the cleanups.

The Air Force is reviewing the case of a Gold Star widow who said she was deemed ineligible for additional benefits following her husband’s death because Congress had not officially declared the military operations in Iran a war.

The Kennedy Center dismantled a famous outdoor sculpture today in an unannounced removal from its grounds.

entries.title: Trump’s Super PAC Is Running Midterm Ads — But They’re All About Trump
entries.summary: Republican lawmakers had hoped Trump would more quickly deploy his reserves to boost candidates ahead of the midterms.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump’s super PAC deployed its first general election advertisements on Wednesday — and almost all of them revolve around Trump.

The two new ads from Securing American Greatness, the MAGA Inc. political action committee’s nonprofit arm, focus heavily on the president and his agenda. Data from tracking firm AdImpact show the spots have begun running in major media markets across the country and cost around $1 million.

The Trump-focused ads come as some Republican lawmakers increasingly voice frustration that the president is not spending more heavily to defend the party’s narrow majority in both chambers of Congress.

Although Trump has signaled he will unleash more money to boost Republicans before November, much of his spending has so far been used to advance his chosen candidates in primaries — including ahead of South Carolina Sen. Darline Graham’s runoff last month.

It’s unclear whether the national ads’ strict focus on Trump will be beneficial to candidates in tight races. Trump’s approval rating has hit record lows during his second term, currently hovering around 33% according to a mid-August Reuters/Ipsos poll. 

One of the advertisements that aired on Wednesday features Ultimate Fighting Championship President Dana White praising Trump. It makes no mention of the Republican congressional candidates on the ballot in November or Republican legislative victories this year.

“He is the toughest, most resilient person that I’ve ever met and nothing was going to stop him from fighting so hard for the country he loves,” White says of Trump before clips of the president’s State of the Union address begin to play.

Another advertisement centers on Republicans’ signature 2025 tax-cut bill, making mention of its most popular provisions including “no tax on tips,” “no tax on overtime” and “no tax on social security.”

But it also spotlights two Trump administration executive orders –– one to lower the cost of prescription drugs and another instructing tech companies to build their own power grids. The advertisement similarly does not explicitly mention Congress or any candidates engaged in tight races this year.

“He’s fighting for you every day,” the ad says as Trump walks on stage. “Help him finish the job.”

The pair of ads aired just days after Senate Majority Leader John Thune implied in an interview with Fox News that Trump could be doing more to support Republicans fending off strong challengers in Senate races across the country.

“I think that they are starting to engage and hopefully will do more as these races start to tighten up,” Thune said of the president’s spending.

entries.title: Rubio Downplays CIA Director’s Surprise Trip to Russia
entries.summary: The secretary of state denied a spate of reports that emerged after CIA Director John Ratcliffe made a rare trip to the country last week.
entries.content:
Secretary of State Marco Rubio brushed off various reports about CIA Director John Ratcliffe’s furtive visit to Russia last week, stating in a Fox News Radio episode aired Wednesday that the spy agency’s leader was there solely to open a dialogue with Russian officials.

Rubio acknowledged Ratcliffe’s visit, which was also confirmed by President Donald Trump in a separate radio interview with conservative political commentator Glenn Beck. At that time, Trump called Ratcliffe’s visit “semi-routine.”

Ratcliffe’s first known trip to Russia as CIA director, which began on Aug. 25, sparked a variety of news reports about what was discussed. According to those reports, discussion topics included a possible trilateral meeting between Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy; a plea for Russia to pursue a peace deal with Ukraine; and a warning against attacking NATO countries.

CBS News first reported Ratcliffe’s trip after a U.S. Air Force jet was seen arriving at a Moscow airport.

Rubio said in the radio interview that he had seen reports about Ratcliffe’s visit but didn’t think any of it was accurate. “Nobody who has any knowledge of that meeting is — it’s a very small handful of people, and none of them have talked to the press.”

Rubio said the trip was “primarily a routine one” that was “not unprecedented.” He added that the United States has to be able to communicate with Russia “from a very practical perspective” and that exchanges between American and Russian intelligence communities have “always existed.”

Ratcliffe’s purpose was to continue to build “intel-to-intel communication channels,” Rubio said, “because things can prove useful in a time of crisis or conflict.”

“This is not unusual; it’s occurred under other administrations as well,” he said.

Ratcliffe has not publicly spoken about his trip. Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov told reporters on Aug. 26 that Ratcliffe met with Russian intelligence officials and did not speak with Putin, who was later briefed on the visit.

entries.title: This Kentucky District Is a Long Shot for Democrats. They’re Prioritizing It Anyway.
entries.summary: If their candidate wins in November, or comes close to it, it would likely signal a broader sweep by Democrats nationally.
entries.content:
There’s little reason to think that a Democratic House candidate in Kentucky’s 6th Congressional District would run any sort of competitive race there.

It’s currently represented by Rep. Andy Barr, who has served since 2013. President Donald Trump won the district in 2024 by 15 percentage points. And Republicans outnumber Democrats in voter registration by about 2,500 voters.

But national Democrats are so sure of their footing ahead of the November midterms that they’re prioritizing it — they recently signaled that they’re willing to pour in resources by adding it to its prized Red to Blue program. It’s one of the most ambitious seats that the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee is hoping to flip this November, and Democrats are banking on an angry electorate to do it.

“They're going to vote for someone who they think is going to help their family and make their lives better, especially when it comes to issues of wages and jobs and affordability, and they don't care about the party,” Zach Dembo, the Democrat running in the district, said in an interview. “There's a strong independent streak that runs through this district.”

This isn’t the only big reach by Democrats. Another one is Tennessee's 5th District, which Trump won by about 23 percentage points. They’re also targeting solidly Republican districts where the incumbents carried baggage, like Rep. Cory Mills’ district in Florida (he lost his primary) and Rep. Nancy Mace’s district in South Carolina (she is not seeking reelection).

If Dembo or the Democrats running in those other districts manage to win in November or even come close, it would likely signal a broader sweep by Democrats nationally.

Barr vacated the seat to run for Sen. Mitch McConnell’s seat in the Senate. The Republican nominee in the district is Ralph Alvarado, a Trump-endorsed candidate who is a former Kentucky state senator and former commissioner of health in Tennessee.

While a long shot for Democrats, even Alvarado’s campaign acknowledges the race could be much tighter than in the past. That it’s an open seat rather than a run against an incumbent is potentially a boost for Democrats.

“It's very much a swing district, and this was always going to be a close race,” an adviser for Alvarado, who requested anonymity, told NOTUS.

Republicans are attacking Dembo as too far left for the district, as Democrats are seeing signs of promise in recent moves Alvarado has taken to distance himself from Trump.

For example, his website no longer mentions Trump in his biography. And a photo of him with the president was replaced on the website’s main page. The adviser said Alvarado is proud of the president’s endorsement, and the changes were made to highlight health care.

“In the general election he intends to talk about the cost of health care and how Zach Dembo will make it more expensive,” the adviser said. The adviser pointed out that the photo of Alvarado and the president remains on the website on another page.

The changes quickly became an attack line for DCCC, which framed it as an effort to “wipe away his ties to Trump.”

Alvarado’s campaign dismissed the changes to the website as having any real effect on the election.

“The socialists are going to have to do a lot better than this nonsense to win this district,” Andy Westberry, Alvarado’s campaign manager, said in a statement.

Dembo, a former federal prosecutor and Navy JAG officer, is making a pitch that Trump’s policies are hurting the red district. More than 25% of people in the district are on Medicaid, gas prices are high, and Canadian tariffs pose risk to the bourbon industry.

His campaign also points to how well Democratic Gov. Andy Beshear did in the district in his 2023 reelection bid. Dembo said he’s counting on Trump voters casting a ballot for him in November, like they did for Beshear.

“My approach to things is very much like Governor Beshear's, which is a nonpartisan, mission-oriented, solutions-oriented idea of, how do we focus on what matters to people in their everyday lives?” Dembo said.

So just how much of a reach is it? Even Democrats in the district were surprised to see Dembo’s name on the Red to Blue list.

“We are gradually giving ourselves permission to feel optimistic,” said Kathy Werking, chair of the Bourbon County Democrats. “It's like, is this really happening?”

entries.title: Thune Distances Himself from Trump on Data Centers and Beef Imports
entries.summary: Interviews Thune has given this week are the latest entries in the rift between the Senate majority leader and Trump after months of tension.
entries.content:
Senate Majority Leader John Thune broke with President Donald Trump on several key policy issues including data center construction, beef imports and the Senate filibuster in interviews this week.

Thune’s recent comments — made two weeks before the Senate resumes business following a recess — are the latest example of a widening policy gulf between himself and the president. Trump has increasingly voiced frustration with Thune’s leadership, particularly as the president’s priority elections bill stalls in the upper chamber ahead of the midterms.

While Thune has trod carefully in his criticism of the president in recent months, he broke with the president on a number of new policy positions this week.

On Monday, Thune implied the White House could do more to support party members engaged in tight Senate races across the country — particularly that of Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, whose race against Democratic nominee James Talarico was shifted left to a “toss up” last month by the Cook Political Report. Spending by Trump’s MAGA Inc. super PAC is still quiet in Texas, even after the president endorsed Paxton in May over incumbent Sen. John Cornyn.

“We’ve got to make sure that those races are resourced,” Thune, who backed Cornyn in the primary, told Fox News. “We are certainly hopeful that the president and his team and MAGA Inc. will be engaged in some of these races. Some states are incredibly expensive.”

Thune’s office declined to comment for this story.

In an interview with a local station in Thune’s home state of South Dakota, the Senate majority leader also broke further with Trump and House Speaker Mike Johnson, casting doubt on their repeated assertions that Republicans expect to keep control of the House and Senate after November’s midterm elections.

“I worry about that for sure,” Thune said Tuesday. “I’m a realist, and I don’t ever try and sugarcoat things. I think it’s a competitive environment right now, I think we got the highest-quality candidates.”

He also reiterated that Republicans do not have the votes to undo the filibuster, which Trump has repeatedly called on Thune to set in motion to advance his voter ID bill. Their disagreement reached a fever pitch in July when then-press secretary Karoline Leavitt told reporters that Trump’s “patience is running out” with Thune.

The Senate majority leader also broke with Trump on local issues: Thune — whose home state ranks fifth in the nation for its number of beef cows — was critical of the administration’s recent move to pause U.S. tariffs on ground beef imports. The new policy drew pushback from some cattle farmers who worry it will undercut domestic beef prices amid a multiyear cattle shortage.

“He’s trying to lower beef prices, which I think we’re all supportive of. I just don’t think this is the way to do it,” Thune told local TV station Keloland on Tuesday. “We have a lot of beef producers here in South Dakota, they produce the highest-quality beef in the world, and we’re trying to build our herds back up.”

Thune pushed back on Trump’s recent call to “let data reign” and embrace the construction of artificial intelligence data centers — an increasingly unpopular stance across both parties that has entered multiple midterm campaigns. The president said Monday that Americans should accept the construction of data centers in their areas unless “they want to end up being backwards and poor.”

The Senate majority leader said companies should not be building those facilities in areas where residents are resistant, although he acknowledged the United States’ race with China to dominate the AI market. South Dakota in March passed a law putting limits on industry construction.

“These entities need to be self-sufficient,” Thune said. “They ought to be able to take care of their own utilities, their own power, and that ought to be a given any place they go in the country. But they shouldn’t be going places where there isn’t support for them at the local level.”

entries.title: Republicans Worry Trump's Oil Meddling Could Stall Venezuela's Elections
entries.summary: Republicans on the House Foreign Affairs Committee want a briefing from the Trump administration on the details.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump’s oil deal with the Venezuelan government has raised red flags among House Republicans who fear that talks with acting President Delcy Rodríguez could ruin the chances of democratic elections in the country.

“I’m looking for more information because I don’t trust [the Venezuelan government],” one House Republican, who was granted anonymity to speak about internal deliberations, told NOTUS. “I think that this is preservation on their part, which I understand, but I don’t like, and what I would love to see is a laid-out time frame of when elections are going to be.”

When Trump announced the framework, the lawmaker said, “I definitely had pause.”

Republicans on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, along with Democrats, are demanding a briefing from the Trump administration to break down how a U.S. majority stake in the oil reserves would work and to provide a timeline for when free elections would take place in Venezuela, NOTUS has learned.

Lawmakers have asked the State Department to explain Trump’s deal, which would give the U.S. control of at least 65 billion barrels of oil, at the House Foreign Affairs Committee’s weekly so-called “hot spot briefings,” the House Republican told NOTUS. Administration officials regularly attend these sessions.

Texas Rep. Joaquin Castro, the top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs’ Western Hemisphere Subcommittee, has also made inquiries to the State Department regarding the Venezuelan oil deal, his office told NOTUS.

The Trump administration is supportive of democratic elections in Venezuela, but has not offered a specific timeline when those would take place.

Earlier this month, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who has led U.S. operations in Venezuela since Nicolás Maduro’s ouster in January, told reporters that “there’s a lot of work that has to happen to lay the groundwork for an election” and that such a process would take “not years, but certainly months and weeks.”

He added that in order for elections to take place, Venezuela must “have an economy and a country whose institutions are functioning, so that they’re not inheriting a disaster, they’re not inheriting a reconstruction process, they’re inheriting a functional state.”

The White House’s fact sheet on the oil deal states that this “investment in Venezuela’s energy sector is a key step in the Trump Administration’s three-part plan of stabilization, reconstruction and democratic transition.”

Still, some Republicans were skeptical about working with Rodríguez.

“I’ve always said that the rule of law needs to be implemented in Venezuela in order for those deals and in order for the big boys in the oil industry in the United States to come to Venezuela. They need to know that the person who is [president] was elected by the Venezuelans, and that’s not the case with Delcy, so we have a glitch there,” Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar (R-Florida), chair of the House Foreign Affairs’ Western Hemisphere Subcommittee, told NOTUS.

“I’m afraid that once Trump is not at the White House ... then Delcy may be still there, and this deal may not continue benefiting the American public,” Salazar said.

When asked if she was concerned that the agreement would eliminate any incentive the U.S. has to replace the current Venezuelan government, Salazar said, “The United States has to have the incentive of behaving according to our Constitution, because we're not in the business of colonizing anybody.”

The U.S., Salazar added, has to give Venezuelans “the platform” to have “free and fair elections.”

“I call Delcy Rodríguez the interim dictator,” Rep. Carlos Giménez (R-Florida) told NOTUS. “What I hear about the oil and the oil deal is actually very good for the United States and also good for Venezuela; I just don’t like too much that we’re dealing with that government. We need to move on from that government.”

Distrusting Rodríguez is one of the rare areas of bipartisan agreement in the House, according to Rep. Gregory Meeks (D-New York), the ranking member of the House Foreign Affairs Committee. He told NOTUS that he “absolutely” wants the State Department to brief members of Congress about the oil deal.

“What [Trump] is doing there is kind of bringing some of us together who really believe and want to promote democracy,” Meeks joked.

Days after announcing the oil deal, the Trump administration received pushback for negotiating with the Venezuelan regime. When the president announced the deal, he said on Truth Social that his administration worked “closely with Highly Respected Interim President of Venezuela, Delcy Rodriguez.”

Since then, other U.S. officials have been doing cleanup.

One U.S. official told NOTUS that the Venezuelan oil deal is “a private deal with a private company. It’s not a deal with the interim government of Venezuela and there was not a political process included in the negotiations.”

“I understand the initial reaction is that we've done a deal with the interim government. The deal is not with the interim government; the deal is with a private entity based abroad,” the official said in a statement. “So this in no way impedes a democratic transition, nor does it mean that it cements the interim government as the government.”

The same official pointed out that the administration has had to work with Rodríguez’s government before: “They are the same people we have to deal with now in order to bring in flights. When American Airlines decided to operate direct flights to Venezuela, we had to work with them. When our delegations visit to help facilitate this democratic transition, the interim authorities are the ones who run passport processing.”

“They are in charge right now of maintaining stability in that country as we work through this transition process,” they continued.

Some Democrats have vowed to investigate the deal if the party gains majorities in Congress in November, Semafor reported.The Defense Department’s Office of Strategic Capital would take a 35% equity stake in North American Blue Energy Partners, which received “100-year concessions for 17 oil fields with proven reserves of approximately 65 billion barrels” from the Venezuelan government, per the White House’s fact sheet on the deal.

A White House official defended the structure, telling NOTUS in a statement: “There can be no transition without a stable economy, and this deal will bring us to a place where elections are possible. This is a country that has been plagued for decades with hyperinflation and virtually zero investment. This privatization helps make a democratic transition possible.”

“It’s worth noting that none of the major opposition leaders in Venezuela have come out to attack this deal — because it’s a good deal for the people of Venezuela and will supercharge their economic recovery,” the White House official added.

Behind closed doors, Republicans have questioned the administration’s actions in Venezuela. In a classified briefing after Maduro’s ouster, Rep. Michael Baumgartner (R-Washington), a member of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, asked administration officials for a specific time frame on when elections would happen, as NOTUS first reported.

Baumgartner told NOTUS that his first reaction to Trump’s Venezuelan oil announcement was “I want to learn more.” But, he added, the deal was “one of the most significant strategic moves that any president has made,” because it would remove Chinese and Russian influence from Venezuela’s oil business.

Four lawmakers — House Foreign Affairs Committee Chair Brian Mast (R-Florida) and Reps. Kat Cammack (R-Florida), Randy Fine (R-Florida) and Jonathan Jackson (D-Illinois) — traveled to Caracas in July to meet with Rodríguez and her brother, Jorge Rodríguez, who is the president of the Venezuelan National Assembly. Based on their meetings, Mast, Fine and Cammack told NOTUS that the Venezuelan government is eager to have a good relationship with the U.S.

Mast told NOTUS that the Rodríguez siblings are “actively working to change the institutions of government that ran the previous elections. So if you want to trust a new election, you’re probably not going to trust that if the people that ran the Maduro elections are still there.” (The 2024 Venezuelan election results, in which Maduro declared himself the winner, are widely considered fraudulent.)

But the Venezuelan opposition is “very much concerned about the likelihood of elections,” Jackson told NOTUS. The Illinois Democrat was the only member of the congressional delegation to Caracas that met with members of the Venezuelan opposition.

Jackson said that Venezuelan opposition members told him they’re concerned that the Trump administration has distanced itself from opposition leader María Corina Machado, including not demanding that she be part of the reconciliation negotiations in the country.

Negotiations between Rodríguez’s government and the opposition are expected to resume in mid-September. The U.S. official said that the Trump administration is “sponsoring” these talks.

The Venezuelan oil deal comes as Americans are facing high oil prices because of the U.S. war in Iran, a major concern for Republicans ahead of the midterm elections.

While Cammack told NOTUS that the deal is “going to bring down gas prices for Americans,” oil industry experts say it will take years for Venezuela’s crude oil to flow into the U.S.

A second House Republican, who was granted anonymity to speak freely, said they trust that Venezuelan elections will happen as long as Rubio remains in charge of the operations in the country.

“If they were to remove Marco Rubio tomorrow, which could happen, because this president, he loves you today and he hates you tomorrow,” the lawmaker told NOTUS, “then I would be worried.”

entries.title: Federal Judge Blocks Trump’s Latest Effort to Restrict Birthright Citizenship
entries.summary: The temporary injunction blocks enforcement of Trump’s executive order targeting “birth tourism.”
entries.content:
A federal judge Wednesday temporarily blocked the administration from enforcing President Donald Trump’s latest restrictions on birthright citizenship against a nationwide class of children, finding that the policy likely violates the 14th Amendment.

U.S. District Judge Deborah Boardman in Maryland said the Supreme Court had already determined that children born in the United States are citizens at birth, even if their parents are unlawfully or temporarily in the country.

“The Supreme Court has spoken: Children in the certified class are ‘citizens at birth,’” Boardman wrote in her 35-page opinion⁠.

The ruling is the latest setback for Trump’s efforts to prune away the constitutional guarantee of citizenship to those born in the United States.

The president issued an Aug. 6 executive order aimed at denying citizenship to some U.S.-born children whose parents are deemed "alien enemies," who work for foreign governments or are part of what the administration calls “birth tourism.”

This is a developing story and will be updated.

entries.title: Election Officials Warn It Could Take Years to Send Out Mail Ballots Under New USPS Rule
entries.summary: The USPS wants each ballot envelope to be scanned individually, with a member of election staff present the whole time.
entries.content:
A former election official did the math on one part of the U.S. Postal Service’s new mail ballot rule, and found it could take years worth of work for Maricopa County, Arizona, to complete one part of the requirements.

The USPS estimated its yet-to-be-deployed ballot-scanning process takes generally less than a minute to verify each outgoing ballot. The county sends out about 2.6 million ballots on the first day of early voting.

“If it took one minute to verify each piece in the mailing, it would take about 4.9 years of continuous scanning to verify the whole mailing,” said Tammy Patrick, the county’s former federal compliance officer for elections and the current chief program officer for the National Association of Election Officials.

As nearly half the states ask courts to block the USPS ballot rules, those officials and other election experts have crunched the numbers on that scanning process to help show why carrying out the president’s mail ballot agenda is implausible in time for the November midterm elections.

The rule stems from an executive order President Donald Trump signed in March. It requires states to submit the name, address and a unique barcode number for every eligible voter to a USPS portal, and then check that each outgoing ballot matches an entry on that list. The USPS said in its final rule that each outgoing ballot envelope must be scanned individually, with a member of election staff present to oversee the entire process.

Ann Jacobs, a former chair of the Wisconsin Elections Commission, looked at just one area, Milwaukee, which mailed out 33,567 ballots for the primary election. At a minute each, that's about 70 days worth of work; if it took 30 seconds each, that's about 35 days worth of work.

“A month of days of someone standing at a post office, watching a scanner. Heck, at 10 seconds each, it's 93.25 hrs or 2 more than work weeks,” Jacobs wrote on social media. “Not to put too fine a point on it, but ballots go out 9/17/26 in Wisconsin - we don't have 35 work days. This is true across the nation.”

In an interview with NOTUS, Jacobs said it would take a long time because the information has to go into an unknown database for matching.

“And they haven't built this database. They haven't built the infrastructure for it or the interface for it,” Jacobs said. “There is no ability of the post office to do what they're proposing, as far as I can tell. There is no indication that they can do this in a timely fashion.”

Hilary Rudy, deputy state elections director in Colorado, said in a court declaration that — using USPS time estimates — it would take more than 66,000 hours worth of work for the agency to scan and cross-reference all 4 million of the state’s mail ballots. According to the Postal Service’s rule, an official from her office would have to remain physically present for that entire time.

Postal officials previously told NOTUS that USPS was rushing its new mailed ballot system without proper testing, which could produce widespread errors and result in disenfranchisement.

A federal court has temporarily blocked the Postal Service from requiring states to participate in the new system, but the mailing agency has said states can still elect to do so.

The Trump administration and some Republican states are appealing that decision, and the Supreme Court could still have the final word before the election in November.

In written testimony provided as part of various lawsuits, local election officials bringing one of the legal challenges said that time spent preparing envelopes for compliance with new USPS demands, uploading voter information into the still-to-come portal for the lists and waiting for the processing of ballots have made compliance with the Postal Service’s new demands a mathematical impossibility.

Dena Dawson, elections director for the Oregon secretary of state, estimated it would take 30 seconds to a minute to prepare each ballot to meet new regulations. In Oregon, all voters automatically receive a mail ballot.

“For 3 million ballots, that is between 25,000 and 50,000 hours of staff time,” Dawson said. “Needless to say, it would not be possible for me to recruit, hire, train, and deploy enough temporary staff to complete that work within the next six weeks, as my existing staff is already overextended with their regular preparations for the November 2026 general election.”

In a statement Tuesday, the Postal Service said it is still in the process of “finalizing the portal” that states will use to submit their voter lists. That is despite a whistleblower this week alleging postal management had set Sept. 1 as a hard deadline for the portal’s “go-live” date.

“The United States Postal Service has spent months developing a U.S. Federal Ballot Mail Portal to provide election officials with a simple, secure, and efficient way to share lists of individuals receiving ballots by mail in their respective states,” USPS said, adding it will provide states “tools, presentations and other resources” before the election.

In the meantime, front-line supervisors who will carry out the new rule are still in the dark. While the rule’s requirements mark a completely new procedure for USPS, postmasters who run the facilities that will receive ballots have yet to receive any guidance for carrying it out, according to a senior Postal Service official familiar with the matter.

According to the whistleblower, USPS’s effort to develop and deploy the portal has been

“rushed,” “risky” and “haphazard” because leadership has set an impossible timeframe. In an effort to meet deadlines, USPS has eliminated standard and needed testing, the whistleblower said, thereby creating substantial risk of a “catastrophic failure” of the system that could “derail the midterm elections.”

The whistleblower added that the USPS IT team working on the project was largely operating without specific details on what they should build, and efforts to gain clarity were unsuccessful. Employees repeatedly raised concerns to leadership, the whistleblower said, but those went unaddressed.

By late August, the whistleblower said, it had become clear that the team would have limited time, if any, to test the product it was building — and would certainly have no time to fix any issues that arose during that testing.

USPS has tasked states with continually updating their lists as voters register, newly become eligible or ineligible, or die. Election officials said in various court filings that would create significant burdens on states, which would have to maintain constant interaction with each jurisdiction within its borders.

“Because ballot requests are usually made directly to local election offices rather than through a centralized state portal, this process will no doubt create delays in enrolling voters and, as a result, delays in mailing and receiving ballots,” said Patrick, the former Maricopa County official.

Rudy, the Colorado official, said that in 2024 her office sent out tens of thousands of ballots after its first batch. Continuing to enroll those individuals in the Postal Service’s portal would add thousands of hours of work for her staff.

"Costs aside, it will be near impossible for counties to complete this work even if they each hired hundreds of temporary employees,” Rudy said.

entries.title: New Jersey Takes Its Fight Against Kalshi to the Supreme Court
entries.summary: Lower courts are split over whether federal law preempts states from regulating sportsbooks.
entries.content:
New Jersey is asking the U.S. Supreme Court to decide whether federal law preempts states from regulating the prediction market platform Kalshi.

In a Wednesday petition to the high court, the state asserts Kalshi has found a federal back door into sports betting, allowing the company to avoid licensing rules, taxes and consumer protections set by individual states.

“Companies like Kalshi claim to offer legal sports betting in all 50 States, but they refuse to follow the gambling laws of any State,” Jennifer Davenport, the New Jersey attorney general, said in a news release.

The company has been bombarded with legal challenges from at least 20 states, but has a fierce defender in the Trump administration. The federal Commodity Futures Trading Commission, headed by Trump appointee Michael Selig, has already sued a handful of states seeking to regulate the prediction market sector.

The issue centers around a dispute over whether Congress, in passing its 2010 Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reform legislation, intended to federalize the multibillion-dollar sports-wagering industry or whether states still hold their traditional regulatory authority over sportsbooks.

"Kalshi is an open, nationwide financial exchange. It cannot be regulated by 50 different regulators," said Kalshi spokesperson Dani Lever. "We remain confident in the lower courts' rulings, and nothing in New Jersey's filing today changes our view."

The request follows a major 9th Circuit Court of Appeals ruling that went against Kalshi, creating a direct split with a separate 3rd Circuit decision that ruled in favor of the company that New Jersey’s state gambling laws are preempted.

The Supreme Court has not yet decided whether it will grant the petition to hear the case.

entries.title: DOJ Says States That Fail to Report Undocumented Immigrants Could Lose Federal Funding
entries.summary: Trump has frequently attempted to withhold federal dollars as a way to ensure so-called sanctuary states comply with his mass-deportation agenda.
entries.content:
The Justice Department sanctioned a powerful new legal tool the Trump administration can use to compel states to assist with the White House’s crackdown on immigration.

The Tuesday opinion by the Office of Legal Counsel sets a framework for the federal government to revoke future welfare grants from states that refuse to report immigrants that did not enter the nation lawfully — another example of the administration threatening to revoke federal funding to force states to provide more data and information about the immigrants who live there.

Funding for federal social services, like Social Security and Temporary Assistance for Needy Families, have largely been dispensed at the discretion of the states since Congress overhauled the national welfare system in 1996. That revamp narrowed certain state reporting requirements in an effort to prevent noncitizens from taking welfare benefits. Previous administrations have agreed that the reporting burden falls only on the specific state agencies that dispense those funds.

The Office of Legal Counsel, which provides legal guidance to the executive branch, reversed that precedent this week.

Dusting off the decades-old, Clinton-era welfare law, Deputy Assistant Attorney General Joshua Craddock concluded in his 19-page opinion that the previous reporting requirements were too “narrow.”

Specifically, Craddock asserts that all agencies in a state that receives welfare grants — which includes every state in the union, as well as the District of Columbia and U.S. territories — must now report immigrants they believe illegally came to the country.

The office’s announcement relies on a revamped interpretation of the word “state” under the 1996 law, retooling it to encompass “all component agencies,” not just the specific agency administering federal benefits.

“The mandatory reporting obligations … thus apply to all agencies within a state that participates in the Temporary Assistance for Needy Families and Supplemental Security Income programs subject to those requirements,” Craddock wrote.

The DOJ said states not currently compliant with the reporting requirements will not lose federal funding that has already been allocated, but future dollars would be jeopardized should state agencies refuse to report undocumented immigrants.

“States remain free to reevaluate their participation in TANF or SSI going forward in view of today’s opinion,” Craddock wrote.

Trump has frequently attempted to withhold federal dollars as a way to ensure so-called sanctuary states and jurisdictions comply with his mass-deportation agenda, but federal judges have consistently ruled against him. More than a dozen states and D.C. have enacted policies aimed at restricting cooperation with federal immigration enforcement. It is unclear how the new federal precedent will clash with those state-level mandates, though some may choose to sue the administration over its new directive.

In July, a coalition of more than two dozen states sued the administration over attempts by the Department of Homeland Security to condition disaster relief and security grants on compliance with immigration and election policies. And in August, a separate group of 20 states and D.C. sued the Justice Department over a similar dispute regarding grants for crime victims.

entries.title: Trump Says White House Helipad Is Complete
entries.summary: The project is estimated to have cost up to $6 million.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump announced Wednesday that a new helipad on the White House grounds is complete, touting the project as both safer and more visually striking than the previous landing area.

Helicopters had been landing on grass at the White House “for many years,” Trump told reporters in the Oval Office. “It’s not good and very unsafe.”

Contractors were asked in early August to redo weeks of construction work after the president reportedly took issue with the landing surface’s appearance and slope. The helipad is estimated to have cost up to $6 million, with defense manufacturer Lockheed Martin covering a majority of the construction cost due to the damage caused by their aircraft.


https://x.com/dannyctkemp/status/2095220114354270585?s=20
Trump praised the work on the new heliport, which he says was finished ahead of schedule and came out “more beautiful than I would have thought.”

“Incredible the job they’ve done,” Trump said. “Carved granite with the seal of the president of the United States.”

entries.title: Trump Is Planning a Midterm Travel Blitz to Alaska and Other Battlegrounds
entries.summary: The president says he expects to campaign heavily in “the last 30 days before the election.”
entries.content:
President Donald Trump said Wednesday he plans to hit the campaign trail ahead of this year’s midterm elections, as lawmakers and candidates increasingly press him to use his political operation — and its massive financial resources — to help Republicans hold their majorities in Congress.

The president also said he will be “making a lot of stops,” adding that he expects to campaign heavily in “the last 30 days before the election.”

He didn’t specify how many states he planned to visit — but he did single out one race he planned to involve himself in: Sen. Dan Sullivan’s reelection battle in Alaska.

“I’ll go out to fight for him,” Trump said, lashing out at Sullivan’s Republican challenger, who also happens to be named Dan Sullivan.

His comments come as Republicans are growing increasingly anxious about the November elections and whether Trump has done enough to help candidates who are struggling.

The president has endorsed candidates in a number of Republican primaries, including several races in which he backed candidates challenging an incumbent.

But Republicans have since raised concerns that Trump has been slower to help some of the candidates he helped elevate, either through in-person campaign trail appearances or shelling out money from his robust political operation.

Party bigwigs have pressed Trump in recent days to help Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, who is locked in a bitter campaign against state Rep. James Talarico for a U.S. Senate seat. The president on Wednesday defended Paxton, who he promised to support moving forward while acknowledging that the Texas Republican has political liabilities.

“The ones we want to focus on will be, obviously, Ken Paxton,” Trump said on Texas Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick’s podcast that aired Wednesday. “We got to get him elected. He’s a good man. You know, I know him very well. He really was a great attorney general.”

Trump went further, saying Paxton’s political weaknesses were largely superficial.

“And some people, I’ll be honest, some people don’t like an interview that he’ll do or something,” Trump said.

Trump doubled down on his assessment in the Oval Office on Wednesday, admitting to reporters that Paxton’s vulnerabilities run deep.

“Some people don’t like the way he dresses, or some people don’t like the way he interviews or talks,” Trump said.

Trump’s political operation has plenty of resources to help his chosen candidates. MAGA Inc., Trump’s main super PAC, had more than $400 million on hand in July, according to campaign finance records.

But the money may not be enough to overcome Republicans’ structural disadvantages this cycle.

Republicans are facing polling showing the president is unpopular among Americans, with a net approval rating of -26, according to an analysis of YouGov polling performed by The Economist.

Polls also show the generic congressional ballot is breaking for Democrats in the ballpark of 6% — with relatively little movement as Election Day approaches, according to election analyst Nate Silver.
